implementation_notes: Java has no user-defined conversions and strictly separates boolean from the numeric types: `int i = 0; boolean b = i;` does not compile, there is no cast between them, and an `if` condition must be boolean or Boolean. The pattern therefore reduces to an API convention - ask the question through a predicate (`boolean isEmpty()`, `boolean hasNext()`) returning the primitive boolean, because a domain object can never be used directly as a condition. Keep flags out of int constants and out of enum arithmetic, and return the primitive rather than the wrapper so the result can never be null.
pitfalls: Use the primitive `boolean`: `Boolean` is a wrapper that can be null and unboxes with a NullPointerException in a condition (the classic `Boolean flag = map.get(k); if (flag) ...` bug).
Storing flags as int (0/1, JDBC/legacy style) reintroduces exactly the mixed arithmetic the pattern prevents; the language rejects bool arithmetic, not int flags.
Bean-style predicates (`isValid()`) are discovered by reflection and serialization tooling, so renaming or changing the return type of a predicate can break frameworks.
